items.stem: Reagan's conservative coalition brought together which of the following groups?
options: (A) Only and exclusively Wall Street bankers, with absolutely no other supporters of any kind whatsoever.
(B) Only active-duty military officers.
(C) Only residents of California.
(D) Business, anti-communists, repudiation voters: united as much by opposition as by favor.
items.explanation: The review supplies all three legs: the tax-cutting, deregulating domestic program for business; the 'evil empire' rhetoric and massive military spending for anti-communists; and the 1980 'repudiation' for voters rejecting the liberal order. Each group got its priority, which is why the coalition held despite their differences.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Business was one leg of the coalition, but the military buildup and the broader repudiation of liberalism drew far wider support.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Anti-communism attracted many civilians; the coalition was not limited to the military.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Reagan won nationally, carrying 44 states in 1980; his coalition was not a regional one.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It assembles the review's three strands — economic, military, and ideological — into the coalition that powered the Reagan era.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan 'promised to shrink government at home — cutting taxes (1981), slashing regulation... while spending massively on the military abroad'; 1980 'repudiation'

items.stem: For ordinary consumers, deregulation's most visible effects in the 1980s included which of the following?
options: (A) The end of all commercial air travel.
(B) Government ownership of the telephone companies.
(C) Cheaper long-distance calls and airfares as market competition replaced government-set rates.
(D) Higher prices for every single deregulated service across the board, without any exception.
items.explanation: Deregulation's consumer payoff was concrete and popular: the breakup-era phone market drove long-distance rates down year after year, and airline deregulation brought discount carriers and fare wars. These visible wins helped sell the broader deregulatory program politically.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Air travel expanded enormously after deregulation; it did not end.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The trend was away from government control — the AT&T breakup being the landmark — not toward ownership.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It names the two textbook consumer benefits of 1980s deregulation: cheaper calls and cheaper flights.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Prices fell in the most prominently deregulated consumer industries, which was the policy's selling point.

items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — Deregulation: 'the rollback of federal rules on business, accelerating under Reagan across airlines, banking, energy, and communications'

items.stem: The chart shows the federal deficit rising from $74 billion in 1980 to $221 billion in 1986. Which criticism of Reaganomics is best supported by the review's own account?

chart_spec.title: Federal Budget Deficit (+) / Surplus (−), 1980–2000
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; Reagan-era deficits per u9.md §The story ('Growth did return, but so did huge deficits').

options: (A) That Reaganomics produced no economic growth whatsoever.
(B) Growth was supposed to pay for the cuts, yet deficits tripled by 1986 — the promise failed.
(C) That Reagan actually raised taxes sharply.
(D) That large and growing federal deficits are actually a sign of fiscal health and good management.
items.explanation: The fairest criticism uses the theory's own standard: supply-side economics promised self-financing growth, and the chart shows the opposite — $74 billion to $221 billion. The review's verdict holds both truths at once: growth returned, but the fiscal promise failed, which is why the deficits belong in any honest assessment.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review states that growth did return; denying it makes the criticism dishonest.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It judges the program by its own central claim and finds it wanting on the chart's evidence — the strongest form of criticism.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Reagan cut taxes substantially; he did not raise them.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Large peacetime deficits were widely seen as a problem, not as a sign of health.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — '"Reaganomics" rested on supply-side theory: lower taxes would unleash growth that paid for itself. Growth did return, but so did huge deficits'

items.stem: 'The new administration finally understands that business creates jobs, not bureaucrats.' — original composition in the style of a 1981 business editorial. A historian using this editorial as evidence for how business viewed Reagan should recognize which of the following?

stimulus.text: The new administration finally understands that business creates jobs, not bureaucrats. — Original composition in the style of a 1981 business editorial.

options: (A) It shows business enthusiasm, but as an interested source: one perspective, not the whole verdict.
(B) It proves beyond any doubt that every single American supported Reagan's entire program enthusiastically.
(C) Business editorials are never valid primary sources for historians.
(D) The editorial was written by the federal government itself.
items.explanation: Sourcing asks whose voice this is: a business publication celebrating a pro-business president. That makes it excellent evidence of business sentiment — the coalition's economic leg — but poor evidence for how workers, consumers, or the economy as a whole fared, which requires other sources.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It applies sourcing properly: identify the perspective, value it for what it shows, and limit claims to what it can support.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. A business editorial speaks for business, not for 'every American'; workers facing concession demands saw the era very differently.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Editorials are standard primary sources for contemporary opinion; they are evaluated critically, not dismissed categorically.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The passage is labeled as a business editorial, not a government document.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan 'promised to shrink government at home — cutting taxes (1981), slashing regulation'

items.stem: Reagan's domestic spending cuts targeted which of the following?
options: (A) Military spending, which was slashed to near zero.
(B) Social Security, which the new administration completely abolished during its very first year in office.
(C) Tax collection, which the administration ended.
(D) Great Society social programs, while defense grew — reversing the 1960s priorities.
items.explanation: The cuts had a philosophy: programs born of the Great Society — antipoverty spending, urban aid, job training, environmental and consumer regulation budgets — were the targets, while the Pentagon's budget soared. It was the New Right's reversal made fiscal: the 1960s had grown domestic government, the 1980s grew military government.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Military spending grew enormously; it was the one budget category clearly exempt from the knife.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Social Security survived; it was too popular to abolish, though Reagan did trim some benefits.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Tax collection continued; the IRS was not abolished.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It describes the actual pattern: domestic social spending cut, defense spending raised — the fiscal expression of the era's reprioritization.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan 'promised to shrink government at home... while spending massively on the military abroad'; §What the exam tests here — the New Right's reversal of the New Deal/Great Society

items.stem: Historians summarizing Reagan's domestic legacy often cite three developments together: the PATCO defeat, large deficits, and rising inequality. What connects the three?
options: (A) All three were caused entirely by foreign governments.
(B) The three had nothing in common with one another.
(C) All three expressed the rebalancing: labor→employers, revenue→debt, middle→top.
(D) All three were pure accidents of history with no relation to any policy choices whatsoever.
items.explanation: The three are one story told three ways. PATCO shifted workplace power toward employers; the tax-cut-plus-buildup fiscal mix shifted government's financing from revenue to borrowing; and both shifts moved income upward. Together they describe what the Reagan revolution redistributed — money and, just as importantly, leverage.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. All three were products of domestic American policy choices, not foreign action.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The three share the era's signature: a systematic shift of power and resources upward and rightward.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It synthesizes the three into the era's single domestic narrative: the rebalancing of power from labor, from revenue, and from the middle.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Each followed directly from deliberate policies: the PATCO firings, the 1981 tax cuts, and the deregulatory program.

items.stem: Franklin Roosevelt held that government must act to secure citizens' welfare; Reagan held that government was the problem. Their core disagreement was over which question?
options: (A) Whether federal power cures economic insecurity or causes it.
(B) Whether the United States should continue to exist.
(C) Whether presidents should be allowed to give speeches to the public at all.
(D) They had no significant disagreement whatsoever.
items.explanation: Strip away the decades and the policies, and the two presidents answered one question oppositely. Roosevelt's answer built the New Deal state; Reagan's answer launched the project of dismantling it. Every specific fight — over taxes, regulation, welfare — was this philosophical disagreement in policy form.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It reduces the Roosevelt-Reagan contrast to its philosophical core, the same contrast the review asks students to draw point by point.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Neither president questioned the nation's existence; they disagreed about government's role within it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Both were celebrated communicators; oratory was not their disagreement.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Their disagreement defined American politics for half a century.

items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — 'Compare Reagan's conservatism with the liberalism it displaced... contrast the two visions of federal power point by point'

items.stem: The chart shows union membership falling from 13.5 percent of workers in 2000 to 10.8 percent in 2020, decades after Reagan left office. What does this continuation suggest?

chart_spec.title: Union Membership as Share of U.S. Workers, 1980–2020
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the long decline following the PATCO turning point described in u9.md §Key terms (PATCO strike, 1981).

options: (A) That Reagan personally caused every single bit of the decline, even in the years after his own death.
(B) Structural economic forces beyond any single presidency drove the decline; PATCO was a landmark within it.
(C) That unions fully recovered their 1980 strength by the year 2020.
(D) That the chart's data must be wrong because declines cannot outlast presidencies.
items.explanation: The chart's post-2000 slide — under presidents of both parties — shows that PATCO lit a fire that structural forces kept burning: the economy's continued shift, global competition, and a legal environment tilted toward employers. Reagan's signal mattered enormously, but the decline's persistence proves it was never only about him.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. A president cannot cause events decades after leaving office; the continuation points to deeper forces.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It reads the chart's full arc properly: a landmark event inside a structural trend, not a one-man cause.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The 2020 value of 10.8 percent is the lowest on the chart, not a recovery.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Long trends routinely outlast the presidencies that start them; the data are consistent with the historical record.

items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — PATCO strike (1981), 'a landmark defeat for organized labor'

items.stem: The chart shows U.S. military spending rising from $134 billion in 1980 to $299 billion in 1990. Reagan cut domestic spending while, in the review's words, 'spending massively on the military abroad.' What does the chart show about his priorities?

chart_spec.title: U.S. Military Spending, 1980–1990 (nominal)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the Reagan-era military buildup described in u9.md §The story ('spending massively on the military abroad').

options: (A) He prioritized domestic social programs over defense.
(B) He cut military spending sharply.
(C) Military strength became the priority: defense doubled while small government was preached at home.
(D) The chart reveals absolutely no discernible priorities or meaningful patterns in the spending data at all, according to analysts.
items.explanation: The chart's more-than-doubling — $134 to $299 billion — is the fiscal proof of the review's phrase. 'Small government' described the domestic side; the military side grew to Cold War peaks. The contradiction was the point: conservatism meant a strong state for defense and a small one for welfare.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Domestic programs faced the cuts; defense received the increases — the reverse of this claim.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The chart shows spending rising steeply, not being cut.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It reads the chart's scale accurately and connects it to the era's defining fiscal asymmetry: military growth amid domestic retrenchment.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. A more-than-doubling over a decade is a very discernible priority.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan 'promised to shrink government at home... while spending massively on the military abroad'

items.stem: The review says Reagan broke the 1981 PATCO strike 'to signal that organized labor's power was over.' What made that signal credible to private employers watching the episode?
options: (A) He praised the strikers and granted all their demands.
(B) He ignored the strike entirely and let it continue.
(C) Congress immediately overruled the president and rehired every single controller with full back pay.
(D) Skilled, irreplaceable strikers broken; traffic kept running. Even strong unions could fall.
items.explanation: Signals work when they're costly. Air-traffic controllers were not easily replaced — yet Reagan replaced them, decertified their union, and banned them from federal service for life. Private employers drew the obvious lesson: if the government could do that to skilled federal workers, they could take a hard line with their own unions — and through the 1980s, they did.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Reagan fired the strikers; he did not meet their demands.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Reagan acted within days, giving the strikers 48 hours to return before firing them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Congress did not overrule the firings; the controllers stayed fired.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It identifies why the example was so powerful: the difficulty of the feat proved the seriousness of the intent.

items.stem: Some historians call Reagan's 1980 victory a 'revolution' rivaling Franklin Roosevelt's in 1932. What is the strongest basis for the comparison?
options: (A) Both repudiated the old philosophy and installed a new answer to what government is for.
(B) Both winning candidates came from the same hometown.
(C) Both elections were decided by the Supreme Court.
(D) Neither of the two elections had any real lasting significance for American governance at all.
items.explanation: 1932 and 1980 are mirror images: Roosevelt repudiated laissez-faire and built the activist state; Reagan repudiated the activist state and began dismantling it. Both elections didn't just change parties — they changed the philosophy of government for a generation, which is what makes 'revolution' the right word for each.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It states the structural parallel the comparison rests on: philosophical repudiation plus a new governing answer, in opposite directions.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Roosevelt was from New York, Reagan from Illinois and California; biography is not the basis of the comparison.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Neither election was decided by the Supreme Court; both were clear electoral victories.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Both elections reshaped American governance for decades; insignificance is the opposite of the historical judgment.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 1980 'repudiation'; §What the exam tests here — 'the New Right reversed the New Deal/Great Society answer to what government is for'

items.stem: The chart shows federal deficits giving way to surpluses by 1998. What ended the Reagan-era pattern of large peacetime deficits?

chart_spec.title: Federal Budget Deficit (+) / Surplus (−), 1980–2000
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the deficit-to-surplus turnaround per u9.md §The story (Clinton 'presided over budget surpluses').

options: (A) The abolition of all federal taxes in 1995.
(B) The elimination of the American military.
(C) The 1990 and 1993 deals (tax hikes plus restraint) plus the surging revenues of the 1990s boom.
(D) The deficits never actually ended at all; the chart is completely misread and shows absolutely no surpluses.
items.explanation: The chart's swing from $290 billion in deficit to $236 billion in surplus came from both sides of the ledger: the 1990 and 1993 deals raised taxes and capped spending — politically costly moves — and the tech-boom economy then flooded the Treasury with revenue. Fiscal balance returned through the very instruments — tax increases and restraint — that supply-side theory had rejected.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Taxes were raised, not abolished; the 1990 and 1993 deals increased revenue.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The military remained enormous; deficit reduction came from taxes, restraint, and growth, not disarmament.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It names the actual policy combination behind the chart's turnaround: bipartisan budget deals plus boom-time revenues.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The chart plainly shows negative values — surpluses — in 1998 and 2000.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Clinton 'presided over budget surpluses'; Reagan-era 'huge deficits'
